title: Austria GP 2026: Practice Sessions Analysis & Race Predictions
summary: Kimi Antonelli heads the aggregated order at the Red Bull Ring with a theoretical 1:06.975, but the top seven are covered by just 0.371s. Our exclusive combined-sector analysis shows Mercedes, McLaren, Ferrari and Red Bull separated by less than half a tenth per sector, with Lando Norris and Charles Leclerc sitting on the largest untapped deltas heading into qualifying.

sections.heading: What the Aggregated Data Reveals
sections.content:
Official timing screens tell you one thing: the fastest single lap a driver managed to string together. That number is useful, but it is also noisy. It is hostage to traffic, to a snap of oversteer at Turn 3, to a yellow flag in the final sector. What it does not tell you is how quick the car actually is. Our aggregated analysis strips that noise out by taking each driver's best Sector 1, best Sector 2 and best Sector 3 across all three practice sessions and summing them into a single theoretical optimal lap. Those sectors can come from different laps, different tyre sets, even different sessions — which is exactly the point.

At the Red Bull Ring that methodology matters more than almost anywhere else on the calendar. The lap is barely 67 seconds long, the sectors are short, and a single compromised corner costs a disproportionate share of the lap. Kimi Antonelli's aggregated 1:06.975 comes from a P2 lap that was already close to complete, while George Russell's 1:07.084 is stitched together from a P2 Sector 1 and a P3 middle-and-final sector. Neither driver ever put that exact lap on the board, but both are demonstrably capable of it — and qualifying is where drivers finally do.

The delta between aggregated and actual is the interesting part. A small delta means a driver is already extracting everything the car has; there is no hidden lap time to find on Saturday. A large delta means the pace exists but has not been delivered yet, usually through traffic, a scruffy sector or a run cut short. Read the two columns together and you get a far better qualifying forecast than the headline sheets provide. This is data you will not find on F1.com, on the FIA timing feed or in the standard session reports — it only exists because we rebuild every driver's weekend sector-by-sector.

sections.heading: The Competitive Picture: Seven Cars, Four Tenths
sections.content:
The aggregated order produces the tightest front group we have seen at this circuit under the 2026 regulations. Antonelli's 1:06.975 leads Russell by 0.109s, Hamilton by 0.189s, Piastri by 0.230s, Norris by 0.264s, Verstappen by 0.341s and Leclerc by 0.371s. Seven cars from four teams inside four tenths, on a lap where four tenths is roughly the length of the run down to Turn 3. On the official actual-lap sheets that spread looks slightly larger at 0.438s, but the shape is identical: nobody has a car advantage here, and qualifying will be decided by execution rather than machinery.

Mercedes are the marginal favourites and the reason is Antonelli. The Italian topped the aggregated order in all three sessions — 1:07.796 in P1, 1:06.975 in P2 and 1:07.057 in P3 — which is the single most consistent signal of the weekend. Russell was never far away and actually produced the fastest genuine lap of Saturday morning at 1:07.096. The W17 looks planted in the final sector, and both cars converted their potential almost perfectly, which is normally the hallmark of a car the drivers trust.

Behind them, Ferrari have quietly had an excellent weekend. Hamilton's 1:07.164 is third fastest and built on the outright quickest Sector 1 of anyone, while Leclerc — who sat out P1 for Dino Beganovic's rookie outing — recovered to seventh on aggregated with the largest remaining delta of the front-runners. McLaren, meanwhile, are split by 0.034s between Piastri and Norris, an intra-team margin so small it is effectively noise. Verstappen sits sixth but with a delta of just 0.053s, which is the polite way of saying Red Bull have already emptied the tank.

Further back the picture is grim for Aston Martin. Alonso's aggregated 1:10.401 and Stroll's 1:10.563 leave the team over three and a half seconds adrift, behind even the Cadillacs of Perez (1:09.453) and Bottas (1:09.521). Whatever direction Aston took into this weekend, the Red Bull Ring has exposed it brutally.

sections.heading: Sector-by-Sector Breakdown
sections.content:
The Red Bull Ring splits neatly into three character tests, and each one crowned a different driver this weekend. Sector 1 — the climb out of Turn 1 up to the crest at Turn 3 — went to Hamilton at 16.577s, set in P3. That sector is dominated by traction out of slow corners and straight-line efficiency up the hill, and Ferrari have clearly found something there: Leclerc was third quickest at 16.652s despite missing an entire session. Antonelli's 16.627s in P2 was the only non-Ferrari inside the top three.

Sector 2 belongs to McLaren, and specifically to Norris. His 29.995s is the only sub-30-second middle sector of the entire weekend, and he backed it up with a 30.004s in P3 — so it was no fluke. Piastri's 30.030s makes it a McLaren one-two in the sector that runs from the crest down through the fast, committed right-handers where aerodynamic stability and mid-corner balance decide everything. That McLaren still only finish fourth and fifth overall tells you exactly where they are losing it: 0.070s to Antonelli in Sector 1 and 0.213s in Sector 3 for Norris.

Sector 3 is Mercedes territory. Russell's 20.224s is the benchmark, 0.083s clear of Antonelli's 20.307s, with Piastri third at 20.381s and Norris only sixth at 20.520s. The final sector is the traction-and-kerb test — Turn 9 and Turn 10 onto the pit straight — and Mercedes are visibly the most settled car over the exit kerbs. Combine that with Antonelli being second fastest in all three sectors, and you understand why he leads the aggregated order without owning a single sector outright: the W17 has no weakness.

The theoretical ultimate lap of the weekend — Hamilton's Sector 1, Norris's Sector 2 and Russell's Sector 3 — is a 1:06.796. Antonelli's aggregated lap is only 0.179s off that composite of three different cars, which is a remarkable indication of how complete the Mercedes package looks around Spielberg.

sections.heading: Tyre Strategy Analysis
sections.content:
Pirelli's softest available trio came to Spielberg, and practice running reflected it: almost nobody at the front bothered with the hardest compound at all. Across the three sessions, Mercedes, McLaren and Ferrari ran a combined zero hard sets between their four race drivers. Red Bull ran exactly one, and that was Hadjar in P3. When the top four teams collectively ignore a compound over three sessions, they are telling you it is not part of Sunday's plan.

The most revealing programme belonged to Antonelli. He got through five medium sets in practice — four of them in P2 alone — against just four softs, by far the most medium-heavy allocation of any front-runner. That is a car being set up around a long first stint on the middle compound, and it dovetails with Mercedes looking strongest in the final sector, where traction and rear tyre management overlap. Russell took a more conventional five-soft, two-medium split.

Verstappen went the other way entirely: eight soft sets in practice against a single medium, including five softs in P3 alone. Red Bull have banked an enormous amount of single-lap data and almost none on the race compound, which is a familiar pattern when a team knows track position will be everything and expects to have to fight for the front row. Leclerc's six-soft, one-medium split in a shortened weekend has the same flavour, though for Ferrari it was as much about catching up on lost P1 mileage as strategic intent.

McLaren split the difference — five softs and three mediums for both Norris and Piastri — which is the profile of a team that genuinely does not know yet whether it is fighting for pole or for the race. Further back, Audi and Alpine were the only teams to invest meaningfully in hard-compound running, with Hulkenberg alone getting through eleven sets in total. Expect a one-stop soft-to-medium as the default at the front, with the hard reserved as an emergency undercut-defence tyre for anyone who loses track position early.

sections.heading: Practice Session Evolution
sections.content:
P1 was an unusually scrappy session because six teams handed a car to a rookie: Beganovic at Ferrari, Iwasa at Racing Bulls, Aron at Audi, Browning at Williams, Hirakawa at Haas and Crawford at Aston Martin. That cost Leclerc, Lawson, Bortoleto, Sainz, Ocon and Stroll a full session of preparation, and it shows in their weekend numbers. Antonelli still led on aggregated with a 1:07.796 from Russell's 1:07.808, but the field was strung out and the track was green.

P2 delivered the fastest running of the weekend as temperatures dropped for the evening slot. Antonelli's aggregated time fell by 0.821s to 1:06.975, and Norris made the single largest leap of anyone, improving from 1:08.673 to 1:07.239 — a gain of 1.434s that transformed McLaren's weekend and produced that sub-30 Sector 2. Verstappen improved by 0.513s, Hamilton by 0.813s. Crucially, P2 remains the reference session: nobody beat their P2 aggregated time on Saturday.

P3 was slower in absolute terms but more revealing. Run in the midday heat, it produced Russell's 1:07.096 — the fastest genuine complete lap of the weekend — and Hamilton's session-topping Sector 1. Ferrari were the biggest movers, with Leclerc appearing for the first time and immediately going sixth on aggregated at 1:07.346. The fact that the front-runners' P3 times cluster within 0.3s of their P2 bests despite significantly warmer conditions suggests the track had rubbered in enough to offset the heat, and that qualifying in similar afternoon conditions should be quicker again.

sections.heading: Key Findings and Surprises
sections.content:
1. Mercedes are the team to beat, and Antonelli is the reason. He topped the aggregated order in all three sessions and finished second fastest in all three individual sectors of the weekend. His 1:06.975 with a delta of just 0.039s to his actual best is the profile of a driver who has already found the limit and is simply waiting for a Q3 tyre.

2. Norris and Leclerc are the two names to watch on Saturday. Norris carries a +0.100s delta and Leclerc +0.106s, the largest of anyone in the top seven. If either strings together the lap our data says they have, Norris drops to a 1:07.239 and Leclerc to a 1:07.346 — enough to reshuffle the entire front two rows. Their raw pace is not the issue; their consistency is.

3. Red Bull have nothing left. Verstappen's +0.053s delta and eight-soft practice programme both point the same way: the car has been wrung out. Sixth on aggregated at +0.341s with no hidden margin is a genuinely difficult starting position, and the encouraging note for the team is that Hadjar sits eighth at 1:07.724 with a delta of just 0.034s — quietly the strongest best-of-the-rest performance of the weekend.

4. The midfield is a mess in the best possible way. Hadjar, Lawson (1:07.901), Lindblad (1:07.995) and Gasly (1:08.059) are covered by 0.335s, with Hulkenberg (1:08.203) and Bortoleto (1:08.256) another tenth and a half back. Lindblad's rookie season continues to impress — he was inside the top seven in P1 and finished the weekend within a tenth of his far more experienced team-mate.

5. The anomaly of the weekend is Aston Martin. Alonso's 1:10.401 aggregated lap leaves him 3.426s off the pace and behind both Cadillacs, and the deficit is spread evenly across all three sectors rather than concentrated in one. That is not a setup problem or a downforce-level choice — that is a fundamental performance gap, and it did not improve meaningfully from P1 to P3.

sections.heading: Race Day Predictions
sections.content:
Qualifying Prediction: expect pole in the 1:06.5–1:06.7 window. Qualifying at Spielberg typically finds three to four tenths over the best practice aggregated time through fuel, engine mode and a fully evolved surface, which puts Antonelli's 1:06.975 potential comfortably under 1:06.8. Our aggregated-based prediction for the top three is Antonelli, Russell and Hamilton, with Piastri a genuine threat at 1:07.205. The wildcards are Norris and Leclerc: both are carrying the largest untapped deltas in the field, and a clean Q3 lap from either would put them on the front row rather than the third.

Race Prediction: Antonelli to convert pole into his win, but not comfortably. The medium-heavy practice programme — five sets, four of them in P2 — points to Mercedes having done more homework on the race compound than anyone, and the W17's Sector 3 advantage is exactly the kind of edge that protects a lead through the DRS zone onto the pit straight. Expect a one-stop soft-to-medium as the default, with the front-runners covering each other on lap 25–32 and the hard compound essentially unused after nobody at the sharp end ran it in practice.

Podium Prediction: 1. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes), 2. Oscar Piastri (McLaren), 3. George Russell (Mercedes). Piastri gets the nod over Russell for second because McLaren's Sector 2 advantage is the hardest place on this circuit to follow closely, and because Piastri's +0.046s delta suggests he is the more repeatable of the two McLarens right now.

Wildcard Factors: Spielberg is one of the most reliable safety-car venues on the calendar — Turn 1, Turn 3 and Turn 4 all combine heavy braking with narrow exits and unforgiving gravel, and lap-one contact at the top of the hill is close to a tradition. With the field this tightly bunched, a mid-race caution would compress everything and hand a free pit stop to whoever has fallen out of position. Afternoon thunderstorms rolling off the Styrian mountains are the other classic variable here and would flip the entire strategic picture.

Dark Horse: Isack Hadjar. Eighth on aggregated at 1:07.724 with the smallest delta of anyone outside the top seven at +0.034s, and a mixed tyre programme including the only hard-compound run of any top-four-team car. He is extracting more from that Red Bull than the headline order suggests, and if the front runners tangle he is the first driver positioned to profit.

Key Battle to Watch: Norris versus Piastri. They are separated by 0.034s on aggregated, they own the two fastest middle sectors of the weekend, and they ran identical tyre programmes — five softs and three mediums each. There is nothing to choose between them on pace, which historically at McLaren means the first corner decides it and the pit wall spends the next seventy laps trying to keep it civil.
